content: Chlorine dioxide (ClO₂) is a chemical compound that exists as a reddish-yellow gas and crystallizes into orange crystals at a temperature of −59°C. It is one of several oxides of chlorine and is recognized as a powerful oxidizing agent. This property makes it highly effective for applications such as water treatment and bleaching. Uses of Chlorine Dioxide Chlorine dioxide is predominantly used (over 95%) for bleaching wood pulp. It is also employed in the bleaching of flour and in the disinfection of municipal drinking water. The first recorded use of chlorine dioxide for drinking water treatment occurred in 1944 at the Niagara Falls water treatment plant in New York, where it was utilized to destroy phenols. By 1956, Brussels, Belgium, adopted chlorine dioxide on a large scale as a drinking water disinfectant, replacing chlorine. In water treatment, chlorine dioxide is commonly used as a pre-oxidant before chlorination. This process helps eliminate natural water impurities that would otherwise react with free chlorine to form trihalomethanes (THMs), which are suspected carcinogenic by-products. Chlorine dioxide is particularly advantageous in water treatment systems operating at a pH above 7, in the presence of ammonia or amines, and for controlling biofilms in water distribution systems. Chlorine dioxide is also widely used in industrial water treatment applications as a biocide, including in cooling towers, process water systems, and food processing facilities. It is less corrosive than chlorine and is superior in controlling Legionella bacteria. Furthermore, it is more effective than chlorine in disinfecting waterborne pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, and protozoa such as Giardia cysts and Cryptosporidium oocysts. However, the use of chlorine dioxide in water treatment results in the formation of chlorite as a by-product. In the United States, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) limits chlorite levels in drinking water to a maximum of 1 part per million (ppm). This restriction confines the use of chlorine dioxide to high-quality water or water treated with iron-based coagulants, as iron can reduce chlorite to chloride. Chlorine dioxide has also been employed for air disinfection and was the primary agent used to decontaminate buildings in the United States following the 2001 anthrax attacks. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, it was used to eradicate hazardous mold from flood-damaged homes in New Orleans and the surrounding Gulf Coast region. Additionally, it is utilized for phenol destruction in wastewater streams, controlling zebra and quagga mussels in water intakes, and odor control in air scrubbers at animal rendering plants. Stabilized chlorine dioxide solutions are sometimes used as oral rinses to treat oral diseases and malodor, though their adverse side effects are still under investigation. Preparation of Chlorine Dioxide Chlorine dioxide is a highly endothermic compound that can decompose violently when not diluted. Therefore, preparation methods that avoid the gas phase are often preferred. In laboratory settings, ClO₂ is typically prepared by oxidizing sodium chlorite. Globally, over 95% of chlorine dioxide production is derived from sodium chlorate, primarily for pulp bleaching. This is achieved by reducing sodium chlorate in a strong acid solution with a suitable reducing agent, such as hydrochloric acid or sulfur dioxide. For disinfection purposes, chlorine dioxide is traditionally produced using sodium chlorite through one of three methods: the sodium chlorite-hypochlorite method, the sodium chlorite-hydrochloric acid method, or the gas-solid method (reacting chlorine gas with solid sodium chlorite). Among these, the chlorite-HCl method produces chlorine-free chlorine dioxide but requires 25% more chlorite to generate an equivalent amount of ClO₂. Handling Properties Chlorine dioxide is unstable at concentrations greater than 15% by volume in air at standard temperature and pressure (STP), where it explosively decomposes into chlorine and oxygen. This decomposition is triggered by light. Its solubility in water increases at lower temperatures, making chilled water (around 5°C) a common storage medium for solutions with concentrations above 3 grams per liter. In many countries, including the United States, chlorine dioxide gas cannot be transported at any concentration and is almost always generated on-site using a chlorine dioxide generator. In some regions, solutions with concentrations below 3 grams per liter may be transported by land, but these are relatively unstable and degrade quickly. Stabilized Chlorine Dioxide Several products marketed as stabilized chlorine dioxide (SCD) do not actually contain chlorine dioxide but consist of buffered sodium chlorite solutions. These can be activated with a weak acid to produce chlorine dioxide in situ without requiring a generator. Recently, a new self-stable formula for stabilized chlorine dioxide has been developed, which is used as a broad-spectrum disinfectant and antimicrobial agent. This form of chlorine dioxide is effective against bacterial and viral outbreaks, including MRSA, Legionella, and Norovirus. SCD is particularly useful when the demand for chlorine dioxide is low and when small amounts of sodium impurities can be tolerated. For applications requiring more than 5 kilograms of ClO₂ per day, chlorine dioxide generated on-site using sodium chlorite or sodium chlorate is typically more economical.
